content: Para-fluorophenylpiperazine (commonly referred to as flipiperazine, fluoperazine, pFPP, or 4-FPP) is a chemical compound classified as a piperazine derivative. It exhibits mild hallucinogenic and euphoric effects and has been marketed as an active ingredient in legal recreational drugs, often referred to as party pills. These substances were initially distributed in New Zealand and later became available in other countries worldwide. Pharmacologically, pFPP primarily acts as an agonist at the 5-HT1A serotonin receptor, with additional binding affinity for the 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C serotonin receptor subtypes. Furthermore, it inhibits the reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine, contributing to its psychoactive properties. The compound was first identified in 1982 as a metabolite of the hypnotic antihistamine niaprazine. However, it was rediscovered in 2003 as a potential recreational drug and subsequently incorporated into party pills sold under brand names such as The Big Grin, Mashed, and Extreme Beans in New Zealand. pFPP has minimal stimulant effects, with its subjective psychoactive properties primarily attributed to its action as a 5-HT1A receptor agonist. Users have described its effects as resembling a combination of fluoxetine (a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) and a very low dose of LSD, both of which also exhibit significant activity as 5-HT1A agonists in addition to their primary mechanisms of action. The effective dose range for pFPP is between 20 mg and 150 mg. However, higher doses are associated with a variety of adverse effects, including migraine headaches, muscle aches, anxiety, nausea, and vomiting.
